subject: biology
title: Sex Chromosomes & X-Linked Traits
welcome_lead: Today you'll see why boys are more likely to be colour-blind — by mastering the XX/XY system and how dad decides the baby's sex.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology sex inheritance — XX vs XY, sex-linked traits (colour blindness, haemophilia), probability crosses.
final_note: You learned that dad's sperm decides the baby's sex, why X-linked recessive conditions hit boys more, and how to calculate sex-linked cross probabilities.

concepts.def: Any chromosome that is NOT a sex chromosome
Trait carried on the X chromosome
Female (Xᴬ Xᵃ) who has the allele but isn't affected

walkthroughs.body_html:
Females are XX. Males are XY.

Mum's eggs always carry an X. Dad's sperm carry X or Y.

So dad's sperm decides the baby's sex — and it's a 50/50 split.

Some genes sit only on the X chromosome — colour blindness and haemophilia are classic examples.

Boys (XY) have only one X. One bad allele = condition shows.

Girls (XX) need two bad alleles. With just one, they're a carrier.

Carrier mum (Xᴬ Xᵃ) × normal dad (Xᴬ Y).

Daughters: half Xᴬ Xᴬ (normal), half Xᴬ Xᵃ (carriers). None affected.

Sons: half Xᴬ Y (normal), half Xᵃ Y (affected). So 50% of sons are colour-blind.

mcqs.q: Which parent's gamete determines the sex of the baby?
Why are boys more likely than girls to be colour-blind?
options: Boys only have one X chromosome, so one recessive allele is enough
The Y chromosome causes colour blindness

numericals.q: A carrier mother (Xᴬ Xᵃ) and an unaffected father (Xᴬ Y) have a son. What is the percentage chance he is colour-blind?
numericals.hint: Sons get the Y from dad and either Xᴬ or Xᵃ from mum

free_texts.q: What word describes a female who carries one copy of a recessive allele but does not show the condition? One word.
free_texts.hint: She can pass it on but isn't affected herself
